blocks.content: 1. Introduction

Think about your old office building. Once you badged in at the front door, you could walk into almost any room. The meeting rooms, the pantry, even the server closet if you knew where it was. Nobody stopped you in the hallway to check your badge again.
That is basically how corporate networks worked for decades. Get past the front door, the VPN, the firewall, and you were trusted everywhere inside.
Zero trust architecture throws that idea out. It says the hallway checks matter just as much as the front door. Every single request, no matter where it comes from, has to prove itself.
This topic walks through why that shift happened, what zero trust actually means in practice, and how you would build it into a real system.
2. The old model: castle and moat
blocks.text: 2. The old model: castle and moat

blocks.content: The traditional approach to network security is usually called castle and moat. You build a strong wall around your network, a moat full of firewalls and VPNs, and you focus almost all your effort on keeping attackers out at that edge.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396368399-214457411.png
blocks.alt: Castle and moat model, perimeter firewall around a trusted internal network

blocks.content: Once a device or a user is inside that perimeter, whether that is the office network or a VPN connection, it is treated as trustworthy by default. Internal traffic between servers, laptops, and services mostly goes unchecked.
2.1 How castle and moat worked

["A firewall and VPN gateway sit at the edge of the network.","Anything outside that edge is treated as hostile and has to authenticate to get in.","Anything inside is treated as friendly. A server calling another server rarely gets challenged.","Access decisions are mostly made once, at the perimeter, not repeatedly inside."]
items: A firewall and VPN gateway sit at the edge of the network.
Anything outside that edge is treated as hostile and has to authenticate to get in.
Anything inside is treated as friendly. A server calling another server rarely gets challenged.
Access decisions are mostly made once, at the perimeter, not repeatedly inside.

blocks.title: Why this felt fine for a long time
blocks.content: When most employees worked from one office, on one network, talking to servers sitting in one data center, the perimeter was a real, physical thing. Trusting everyone inside it was a reasonable shortcut.
2.2 The hidden assumption
Castle and moat quietly assumes that the inside of your network is a safe place. It bets everything on the wall holding. As long as no attacker gets past the firewall, you are fine.
The hard part was keeping attackers out. Nobody spent much energy worrying about what happens once someone is already in.
3. Why the old model broke down
blocks.text: 3. Why the old model broke down

blocks.content: Two things happened that castle and moat was never designed for: the network stopped having a clean edge, and breaches stopped being rare.
3.1 There is no clean perimeter anymore
blocks.text: 3.1 There is no clean perimeter anymore

blocks.content: Your app is not sitting in one data center behind one firewall anymore. It is spread across cloud providers. Your employees work from home, from coffee shops, from their phones. Contractors and partners need access too.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396368400-752728593.png
blocks.alt: Remote employees, cloud SaaS apps, and mobile devices all reaching company services over the open internet

blocks.content: ["Cloud services live outside any network you physically control.","Remote work means employees connect from home wifi, airports, anywhere.","Mobile devices blur the line between personal and corporate even further."]
items: Cloud services live outside any network you physically control.
Remote work means employees connect from home wifi, airports, anywhere.
Mobile devices blur the line between personal and corporate even further.

blocks.content: So the question "is this request coming from inside the network" stops meaning very much. There often is no single inside anymore.
3.2 Lateral movement: what happens after a breach
blocks.text: 3.2 Lateral movement: what happens after a breach

blocks.content: The bigger problem shows up the moment castle and moat fails even once. If an attacker steals one employee laptop, one set of credentials, or one exposed internal service, castle and moat hands them the whole inside of the network to explore.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396368400-983903295.png
blocks.alt: Attacker breaches the perimeter through one compromised laptop, then moves freely to finance, HR, and admin systems

blocks.content: This is called lateral movement. The attacker is inside the moat now, so nothing stops them from hopping from that laptop to a file server, to a database, to an admin panel, quietly expanding their access.

blocks.title: The real cost of castle and moat
blocks.content: It is not that the wall gets breached. Walls sometimes get breached no matter how good they are. The real cost is that one breach anywhere inside used to mean access everywhere inside.
4. The zero trust principle: never trust, always verify
blocks.text: 4. The zero trust principle: never trust, always verify

blocks.content: Zero trust flips the entire assumption. Instead of trusting requests because of where they came from, it verifies every request on its own merits, every single time.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396368401-718472069.png
blocks.alt: Every incoming request passes through a verification step before reaching the service, regardless of origin

blocks.content: It does not matter if the request is coming from an employee laptop on the corporate wifi, a server in your own data center, or someone on the public internet. None of that location information grants any trust by itself.

["No request is trusted just because it came from inside the network.","Every request must be authenticated, confirming who or what is making it.","Every request must be authorized, confirming it is actually allowed to do what it is asking to do.","This check happens on every request, not once at login and never again."]
items: No request is trusted just because it came from inside the network.
Every request must be authenticated, confirming who or what is making it.
Every request must be authorized, confirming it is actually allowed to do what it is asking to do.
This check happens on every request, not once at login and never again.

blocks.content: Never trust, always verify. Location tells you nothing about intent.
5. The building blocks of zero trust
blocks.text: 5. The building blocks of zero trust

blocks.content: Never trust, always verify is a principle, not a product you install. Here are the practical pieces that make it real.
5.1 Strong identity verification per request

Instead of one login that grants a long lived session with broad network access, zero trust systems verify identity on every request, usually with a short lived token rather than a long lived network level trust relationship.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396368401-589859707.png
blocks.alt: Long lived network trust grants wide open access, while short lived tokens grant narrow, timed access

blocks.content: If a token leaks, the damage window is small because it expires soon. Compare that to a VPN session or a static network credential that might stay valid for weeks.
5.2 Least privilege access

A verified identity should only get the narrowest set of permissions it actually needs for the task at hand, nothing more. An engineer debugging a payments issue does not need write access to the user database.

["Grant access to specific resources, not entire networks.","Scope tokens down to exactly the actions they need to perform.","Review and shrink standing permissions regularly instead of letting them accumulate."]
items: Grant access to specific resources, not entire networks.
Scope tokens down to exactly the actions they need to perform.
Review and shrink standing permissions regularly instead of letting them accumulate.

blocks.content: 5.3 Continuous verification

A one time login is not trusted forever. Zero trust systems keep checking. Did the device posture change? Is the token still valid? Is this request pattern normal for this user? Trust is something you keep earning on every request, not something you bank once at sign in.
5.4 Micro segmentation

Even internal services do not get a free pass to talk to each other. The network is broken into small segments, and any service calling another service has to authenticate itself first, exactly like an external request would.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396371089-378268153.png
blocks.alt: Service A authenticates to reach Service B, Service B authenticates to reach Service C, direct unauthenticated hops are blocked

blocks.title: This is the direct fix for lateral movement
blocks.content: If every internal hop needs its own authentication and authorization, a compromised service can no longer just wander sideways through the rest of the network the way it could under castle and moat.
6. Tying it to mTLS, RBAC, and short lived credentials
blocks.text: 6. Tying it to mTLS, RBAC, and short lived credentials

blocks.content: Zero trust is not one single technology. It is a design philosophy that leans on a handful of concepts you have probably already run into separately.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396371091-695989880.png
blocks.alt: mTLS, RBAC, and short lived credentials all feed into a single zero trust allow or deny decision

blocks.content: {"headers":["Concept","What it gives zero trust"],"rows":[["mTLS between services","Both sides of a connection prove their identity with certificates, so a service knows exactly which other service it is talking to, not just that traffic arrived on the internal network."],["RBAC","Fine grained authorization. Even after identity is confirmed, RBAC decides exactly which actions that identity is allowed to perform."],["Short lived credentials","Tokens and certificates that expire quickly, so a leaked credential is only dangerous for a short window instead of indefinitely."],["Service mesh","A common place to enforce mTLS and authorization policy consistently across every service, without every team reimplementing it."]]}
Put together, these pieces are what make never trust, always verify practical to actually run at scale, instead of just a slogan.
7. Real world usage

Zero trust is not a theoretical idea. Google famously moved its entire internal infrastructure this way after realizing that VPN based perimeter security was not enough for a company operating at their scale and under constant attack.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396371092-426547974.png
blocks.alt: BeyondCorp style architecture: device inventory and identity checks feed an access proxy that fronts every internal app

blocks.content: Their approach is called BeyondCorp, and it is widely cited as the original well known real world implementation of zero trust. Instead of a VPN, every request to an internal application goes through an access proxy that checks user identity and device trust before letting anything through, regardless of whether the request came from inside a Google office or from a random coffee shop.

["No VPN. Employees can work securely from anywhere without connecting to a special trusted network first.","Access decisions depend on who you are and what device you are using, not which network you are physically on.","Many modern cloud native companies now architect around this by default rather than treating it as an add on."]
items: No VPN. Employees can work securely from anywhere without connecting to a special trusted network first.
Access decisions depend on who you are and what device you are using, not which network you are physically on.
Many modern cloud native companies now architect around this by default rather than treating it as an add on.

blocks.content: 8. Worked example: redesigning an internal admin tool
blocks.text: 8. Worked example: redesigning an internal admin tool

blocks.content: Say your company has an internal admin tool used to manage customer accounts, refunds, and support tickets. The old version trusts anyone connected to the company VPN. Once you are on the VPN, the tool just lets you in, no further questions asked.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396371093-168530339.png
blocks.alt: Old design: anyone connected to the VPN is implicitly trusted by the admin tool

blocks.content: This is a classic castle and moat setup, and it has an obvious problem. If any employee laptop on that VPN gets compromised, or if the VPN credentials leak, the attacker now has full access to customer data and refund controls.
8.1 The zero trust redesign

The team redesigns the tool so the VPN stops mattering for trust decisions. Every request, even one coming from inside the VPN, must present a valid short lived token tied to a real employee identity, and it must pass an authorization check for the specific action being requested.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396371093-304012781.png
blocks.alt: New design: every request presents a token and passes an authorization check before reaching the admin tool

blocks.content: ["Login issues a short lived token, not a long lived session cookie or static API key.","Every request to the admin tool carries that token and gets verified fresh.","Authorization checks the specific action, so a support agent can view tickets but cannot issue refunds.","Being on the VPN no longer grants any special trust by itself."]
items: Login issues a short lived token, not a long lived session cookie or static API key.
Every request to the admin tool carries that token and gets verified fresh.
Authorization checks the specific action, so a support agent can view tickets but cannot issue refunds.
Being on the VPN no longer grants any special trust by itself.

blocks.title: What this buys you
blocks.content: If an attacker steals a laptop or even the VPN credentials, they still cannot do anything in the admin tool without a valid, narrowly scoped token, and that token expires soon anyway.
9. Implementation: enforcing zero trust at the request level
blocks.text: 9. Implementation: enforcing zero trust at the request level

blocks.content: Here is a simplified version of what that authorization check looks like in code. Notice it never asks anything about network location. It only cares about the token and what that identity is allowed to do.

The key detail is what is missing. There is no check for a trusted subnet, no allowlist of internal IP ranges, nothing that says requests from the VPN skip verification. Every single call earns its access the same way.

blocks.title: Gotcha: do not let internal traffic bypass this
blocks.content: It is tempting to add a shortcut like "skip auth if the request is from our own internal network" for convenience. That single shortcut recreates castle and moat inside your zero trust system and reopens the door to lateral movement.

blocks.title: Gotcha: token lifetime is a real tradeoff
blocks.content: Too short and you hurt usability with constant re-authentication. Too long and you lose most of the benefit over a traditional session. Most real systems land somewhere in the minutes to low hours range, paired with silent refresh.
10. The interview angle
Zero trust is a strong, current answer whenever an interview question leans security heavy, especially around internal tooling, remote access, or a security conscious enterprise customer.

["If asked to design an internal admin panel or support tool, mention per-request authentication instead of relying on VPN or network location.","If asked about a company with a remote or hybrid workforce, zero trust explains how you would replace a traditional VPN based access model.","If the interviewer mentions an enterprise customer with strict security requirements, zero trust concepts like short lived credentials and least privilege signal you understand modern security expectations.","Being able to name mTLS, RBAC, and micro segmentation as the concrete pieces behind the buzzword shows depth beyond just repeating \"never trust, always verify\"."]
items: If asked to design an internal admin panel or support tool, mention per-request authentication instead of relying on VPN or network location.
If asked about a company with a remote or hybrid workforce, zero trust explains how you would replace a traditional VPN based access model.

If the interviewer mentions an enterprise customer with strict security requirements, zero trust concepts like short lived credentials and least privilege signal you understand modern security expectations.
Being able to name mTLS, RBAC, and micro segmentation as the concrete pieces behind the buzzword shows depth beyond just repeating "never trust, always verify".

blocks.content: You do not need to reinvent BeyondCorp in an interview. You just need to show you know why perimeter only security fails and what specifically replaces it.
11. Summary
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396371093-292191168.png
blocks.alt: Castle and moat trusts by location, zero trust trusts by continuous verification

A single bypass shortcut for internal traffic undoes the whole model"]]}

Castle and moat asks one question once: did you get past the wall. Zero trust asks the same question on every single request: should this specific action, by this specific verified identity, be allowed right now. That shift is what makes it hold up in a world without clean network edges.
